answer:
This is so much harder today than it used to be, but many of you are still doing it. And most importantly, you should know how it works. It’s not as simple as “if they buy from us.” That part we’ve worked out over time. But what I’ve seen founders misunderstand again and again is the social contract between them and their customers. What do I mean by that? A lot of startups sell primarily to end-users these days. So they often have no idea on Day 0 what enterprise buyers’ needs really are:
What will happen if they lose data?
How secure does this product need to be?
How easy is deployment? How hard is removal?
Can our app integrate with others already in production?
Is your code base stable enough for mission-critical apps?
Does this vendor have real support? Real security experts?
The list goes on and on. There are so many reasons why enterprises don’t want to use startups. They can’t handle loss of data or functionality. Or downtime. Or any risk at all when business continuity is critical. In fact, 80%+ of start-ups just aren’t ready to sell into the enterprise. Many can’t even get past a pilot! But some are ready, especially those selling to SMBs and mid-market companies. Especially SaaS ones. Because SaaS apps are now everywhere. And the more you understand that social contract above, the better chance you’ll have. More here:
If Your App Is Going To Be Secure … Why Would Any Enterprise Buy From You? | SaaStr

So one of our favorite SaaS companies is Monday.  We’ve covered them so many times on SaaStr over the years and I was fortunate enough to interview their founders way back when they were just getting going.
They IPO’d in June 2021 as part of a batch of Cloud leaders that included SailPoint and others, and have since grown into a real force in work management — crossing $500m+ ARR with an impressive 45% growth rate:
Monday’s NRR is very healthy at 115%, and it has almost no churn (just 0.2%), which isn’t surprising given its high end customers pay $100k-$300k+ per year for their platform.  It also serves SMBs and mid-market companies well too, but it takes longer to get there than larger enterprise deals.

.  This makes sense, as most of us use Asana, Notion, etc. now. #2.  65% of Revenue From “Platinum” Edition or Higher; 80% of New Business is Platinum+
.  Monday sells different editions with varying amounts of functionality.

Dear SaaStr: What Are Some Tips for Standing Out at an Interview? Well, if you want to stand out in any interview — send your stuff ahead of time. Most importantly, make sure it is great. Here’s how to do that:
Make Sure Your LinkedIn is Strong. Do this before every job interview
. No excuses. It takes 20 minutes. Make sure everything here is strong and up-to-date. If nothing else, spend some time on the company page. Like their products, like what they are doing. That shows engagement right there.
Send Over All The Stuff Ahead Of Time
. Again, no excuses. Send over references ahead of time. A resume ahead of time (not via Indeed). Write up why you would be great for the role ahead of time. Share them all. And share them with as much detail as possible. Do this ahead of each interview. It will show you truly care. More
here
.
Do Real Homework. Show You’ve Done This Before Every Interview
. I know you haven’t read every single thing written by the CEO or everyone on the leadership team. But pick one or two things you really think you could add value to. Ask thoughtful questions about those topics during the interview. Show you have done real homework. Not just copied off Wikipedia or a few tweets.
Ask About The Top Challenges, and How You Can Help Solve Them
. Everyone knows their top challenges. At least ask. It also gives you a chance to talk about yourself and how you can help solve some of them. More
here
.
Show Up Early
. Show up early for interviews. Even if you don’t need to. It makes such a good impression. Bring Coffee. Or Pastries. Or Both. Don’t worry too much about being late or running a bit behind. Just bring something nice.

answer:
Dear SaaStr: I’m seeing too many high-growth B2B companies with low net retention rates. How can I keep my customers and increase revenue?
First, let’s be honest here. Net Retention Rate is the most important KPI for any B2B company, period.
If you have mediocre growth, that’s OK. But if your NRR is <100%, then something is fundamentally wrong at least until $10m-$20m ARR or so, when it may be OK as long as growth overall remains strong. Even today, there are still plenty of unicorns growing <80% on top of 110%-120%+ NRRs.
It’s not just the money (although it’s a lot). It means you aren’t solving real customer problems. And worse, even worse — you don’t know how to do it well enough yet. Or maybe ever.
So what should you do?  First, figure out why your NRR isn’t where it needs to be:
Are you losing deals in sales due to product gaps? That’s a sign you need to build more. Are you losing deals in renewals because upsell hasn’t happened? That’s a sign you haven’t built the right team yet. Is churn up from support issues? That’s a sign you need better CS. Is churn up from lack of expansion opportunities? That’s a sign you need to add more value. Whatever it is, fix it. Because if your NRR is <100%, you’re probably dying. Slowly, but surely.
Second, set an annual target of improving it by say -15%. So if you have 90% NRR today, aim to get to 105% next year. Then make sure everyone knows this is their #1 goal.
Third, if you really want to grow faster than before, you’ll have to find new ways to retain customers. This might mean hiring a VP of Customer Success who can turn things around quickly.

.  They just need to understand accounting better and/or are honest enough to admit when they aren’t sure of something.

And then Phase Two kicks in once you’ve proven that your AI SDR actually works, which you will be able to measure — and then bring humans into the process. Once you have qualified leads, inbound opportunities, or enough pipeline volume, phase two begins. At that point, the goal shifts dramatically—you want your AI SDR to hand off seamlessly to a human who knows everything about that lead. You want the handoff to be smooth.

answer:
Dear SaaStr:  How do you deal with angry customers?
It’s not fun, but …
There are 2 types of customers. Happy ones and unhappy ones. Unhappy ones will complain.
They may leave, or they may stay. But if nothing else, it’s your job as CEO to make sure every customer leaves happy. Even if that means sometimes letting them go if you can’t solve their problems.
So here are my top learnings:
First, be present
. Go visit all your existing customers at least twice a year for real. They’ll know — and so will you. If you don’t show up in person once a quarter, you won’t get enough feedback on what matters most.
Second, listen more than you talk
. Listen to every complaint, every question, etc. Do this in-person, too. And just listen, without interrupting. Without making excuses. Without being defensive. And then respond thoughtfully.
Third, give upgrades
. You should always have a few extra licenses available to upgrade an unhappy customer for free. Or to extend their contract, even if it’s short-term. It doesn’t cost much relative to churn-and-burn costs down the road.
Fourth, fix it
. Whatever it is. If you’re late shipping? Fix it. If you missed a feature request? Build it. If you didn’t deliver on time? Deliver now. If you lost their data? Get it back. Just fix it.
Fifth, apologize
. Apologies aren’t magic. They don’t magically turn bad things into good. But they help. A lot. In B2C, apologizing often works well because there isn’t any long relationship, per se. We’ve seen many examples where a simple apology has saved an account. But also remember, no one wants another problem on top of the one they already have.
Sixth, ask yourself: would I buy from us again if we were smaller? This is important. Would you buy your own product again today?

I think this is a good question, but it’s also somewhat irrelevant.
A CMO (Chief Marketing Officer) isn’t just someone to own marketing. They are often really a VP Product and GTM with an understanding of how product-market fit scales into revenue growth.
They need to be able to:
Own pipeline generation across all channels — from brand to field marketing to digital demand gen to content marketing to events
Hire a team that can do most or even all of this, ideally under them
Partner closely with sales, customer success, and others on the leadership team
Bring up new VPs as they scale
Manage multiple stakeholders internally and externally
Build processes to manage these areas at scale
Do competitive intelligence and positioning strategy
And much more …

If your startup has no one doing any of this stuff well yet, then don’t hire a CMO. You’ll only set yourself up for failure by hiring someone who needs resources she doesn’t have access to yet.

That person will bring the discipline, process, and executive-level thinking needed to get everyone rowing in the same direction while scaling each function properly.
